name: Testicular germ cell tumour (overview)
aliases: germ cell tumour of the testis

clinicalPearls: Typically presents as a painless, firm, unilateral testicular mass or diffuse enlargement in a young or middle-aged man, and any solid intratesticular lesion is malignant until proven otherwise
Germ cell tumours are broadly divided into seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (NSGCT), a distinction that drives staging, treatment, and follow-up

Serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) should always be measured before and after treatment: seminoma may raise beta-hCG and LDH but keeps a normal AFP, whereas a raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element regardless of histology
A history of cryptorchidism (including the contralateral, normally descended testis), prior contralateral tumour, family history, and infertility are recognised risk factors
Scrotal ultrasound is the first-line imaging test and radical inguinal orchidectomy is the standard approach for diagnosis and local control; trans-scrotal biopsy is avoided to prevent tumour seeding
Sperm banking should be offered before orchidectomy or systemic therapy because both the disease and its treatment threaten fertility
Staging with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis assesses retroperitoneal nodal and visceral spread, and post-orchidectomy marker kinetics guide risk stratification
reference.pathophysiology: Most testicular germ cell tumours arise from a precursor lesion, germ cell neoplasia in situ, in which malignant transformation of primordial germ cells within the seminiferous tubules is thought to begin in fetal life. Progression yields either seminoma, which resembles undifferentiated germ cells, or non-seminomatous tumours that recapitulate embryonic and extra-embryonic differentiation (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, teratoma), often as mixed tumours. Isochromosome 12p is a characteristic cytogenetic marker. Spread is typically lymphatic to the retroperitoneal nodes following gonadal drainage, with later haematogenous dissemination to lung and other viscera; choriocarcinoma has a particular tendency to early blood-borne spread.
additionalDifferentials: Epididymo-orchitis or an inflammatory testicular mass
Testicular lymphoma, especially in older men
Sex cord-stromal tumours (Leydig or Sertoli cell tumour)
Testicular torsion presenting as acute swelling
Metastasis to the testis from another primary
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to confirm an intratesticular solid lesion
Serum tumour markers AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH before and serially after orchidectomy
Radical inguinal orchidectomy for histological diagnosis and local control
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for nodal and visceral staging
Semen analysis and sperm banking prior to treatment
MRI or brain imaging when choriocarcinoma or neurological symptoms raise concern for cerebral metastases
redFlags: Bulky retroperitoneal disease or a supraclavicular node indicating advanced spread
Respiratory compromise or haemoptysis from pulmonary metastases
Very high beta-hCG with gynaecomastia or thyrotoxic features suggesting large tumour burden
Neurological symptoms raising suspicion of cerebral metastases from choriocarcinoma
Markers that fail to normalise after orchidectomy, indicating residual or metastatic disease
reference.prognosis: Testicular germ cell tumour is among the most curable solid malignancies; the great majority of patients, including many with metastatic disease, achieve long-term cure with stage-appropriate surgery, surveillance, cisplatin-based chemotherapy, or radiotherapy, though prognosis worsens with high-risk marker elevation and non-pulmonary visceral metastases.
pitfalls: Mistaking a tumour for epididymo-orchitis and delaying ultrasound and orchidectomy
Performing a trans-scrotal biopsy or orchidectomy and risking tumour seeding and altered lymphatic drainage
Omitting pre-treatment tumour markers, losing prognostic and monitoring information
Failing to offer sperm banking before orchidectomy or chemotherapy
Overlooking a small contralateral lesion or the increased contralateral risk in men with cryptorchidism
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy for histological diagnosis and local control, avoiding trans-scrotal biopsy to prevent tumour seeding
Offer sperm banking before orchidectomy or systemic therapy given the fertility threat from disease and treatment
Measure serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH before and serially after orchidectomy to guide staging, risk stratification and monitoring

Tailor treatment to seminoma-versus-non-seminoma histology and stage: active surveillance for many stage I tumours, cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy for metastatic disease, and radiotherapy as an option for seminoma
Consider retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection for selected non-seminomatous disease and resect residual post-chemotherapy masses
Maintain prolonged surveillance for relapse and a metachronous contralateral tumour, with androgen replacement if hypogonadism develops
Manage within a uro-oncology multidisciplinary team
